title: Throat tightness after shared trail mix in a nut-allergic hiker

source.title: Case Study: Anaphylaxis in the Backcountry

classification.acuity_basis: Airway symptoms requiring epinephrine; risk of biphasic reaction with no second dose; PLB activated, SAR evacuation.

context.distance_to_care: deep in wilderness; SAR responded in 40 min

pertinent_history: prior reaction needing epinephrine 1 year ago

presentation.summary: Minutes after eating shared trail mix said to be nut-free, a hiker develops throat tightness, tingling and trouble swallowing that worsen over 20 minutes. Self-injects epinephrine into the thigh.
symptoms: after epinephrine: mild tingling, nausea, nervousness

plan: activate PLB and wait for rescue
remove all group food from patient
if no response in 1 h, start hiking toward trailhead
teaching_points: Epinephrine is first-line; don't delay it for antihistamines.
Give epinephrine for airway swelling (lips, tongue, voice change), breathing difficulty, widespread swelling, or shock. Adult IM dose 0.3 mg (0.3 mL of 1:1000).
Give oral antihistamine when able to swallow and continue during evacuation.
If symptoms return, give more epinephrine and evacuate.
Carry two epinephrine doses; manage group food cross-contamination.

must_ask: throat tight, voice change, trouble breathing or swallowing?
do you have an epinephrine auto-injector? a second one?
known allergies?
eval.must_escalate: Give epinephrine immediately and evacuate even if symptoms improve.
must_not_recommend: continuing the hike after epinephrine without evacuation plan

lay_queries: my throat feels tight after eating trail mix and I'm allergic to nuts
she used her epipen now what

title: Boiling water spilled into a boot: leg and heel burns

source.title: Case Study: Burn in the Backcountry

classification.acuity_basis: Partial-thickness foot burn; walked out over a day for evaluation.

context.distance_to_care: 1 day hike to trailhead; stream 200 m from camp

presentation.summary: A student trips carrying a pot and boiling water pours into another student's boot.
presentation.chief_complaint: burn pain left leg and heel
exam_findings: ~5% TBSA superficial burn back of left lower leg
2x3 in partial-thickness heel burn, blister ruptured

plan: cool irrigation
dress partial-thickness burn with hydrogel and gauze
walk out in running shoes with heel folded down
teaching_points: Depth: superficial red/painful; partial thickness blisters; full thickness pale/charred/painless.
Palm with fingers ~1% TBSA.
Evacuate all full-thickness burns; consider for partial thickness on hands, feet, face, armpits, groin.
Rapid evacuation: >10% TBSA partial/full, circumferential, or airway burns (face/neck burns, soot, singed hair, cough).
Cool water irrigation; no ice; watch for hypothermia in large burns; don't drain intact blisters; non-adherent dressings changed twice daily.

outcome.summary: Walked out slowly; healed; hiking again in weeks.

must_ask: how big is the burn compared to your palm?
are there blisters? white or charred areas?
any burns to face or airway?
eval.must_escalate: Rapid evacuation for >10% TBSA, circumferential, airway, or full-thickness burns.
must_not_recommend: butter or ointments on fresh burns

lay_queries: spilled boiling water on my foot
burn on my leg with blisters while camping

title: Young angler with sudden chest pain and breathlessness at 8,500 ft

source.title: Case Study: Shortness of Breath While Fishing

classification.acuity_basis: Respiratory distress; helicopter evacuation; confirmed pneumothorax.

context.distance_to_care: 20 min hike to cell signal; meadow LZ nearby

presentation.summary: While fly fishing, a young man gets sharp right upper chest pain he thinks is a pulled muscle; 90 minutes later he becomes short of breath, speaking in short sentences with labored breathing.
presentation.chief_complaint: shortness of breath and chest pain
symptoms: sharp right chest pain then pressure/tightness
exam_findings: no audible breath sounds by ear to chest

assessment: shortness of breath; possible spontaneous pneumothorax or pulmonary embolism
plan: position of comfort
monitor vitals
keep calm
evacuate ASAP: call from ridge, prepare meadow LZ, signal mirror
teaching_points: Spontaneous pneumothorax: tall thin young men, often at rest, sudden sharp chest pain then worsening SOB.
PE risk: immobility, long travel, dehydration, altitude, smoking, recent surgery; sudden SOB, pleuritic pain, fast HR/RR.
Diminished breath sounds on one side suggest pneumothorax.
Respiratory distress is a life threat requiring prompt evacuation.

outcome.summary: Flight medic found diminished right breath sounds, oxygen and IV; pneumothorax confirmed; 1-2 day stay.

must_recognize: non-traumatic chest pain with SOB is an emergency
pneumothorax vs PE vs muscle strain
must_ask: did it start suddenly?
is breathing getting worse?
pain when breathing in?
any leg swelling, recent long travel?
must_not_recommend: treating as a pulled muscle and continuing

lay_queries: sudden sharp chest pain and now I can't catch my breath

title: Teen with known asthma wheezing at the top of a steep climb

source.title: Case Study: Breathing Difficulty in the Absaroka Range

classification.acuity_basis: Responded to albuterol within 20 min; observed overnight; trip continued.

presentation.summary: At the top of a long steep climb a teen kneels in tripod position, wheezing, anxious, fumbling with his inhaler. Says it feels like his asthma.

assessment: possible hyperventilation or other respiratory problem
plan: calm, slow breathing, help with inhaler
move from triggers
albuterol 2 puffs per label
continue with monitoring if resolves; evacuate if recurrent or unresponsive
teaching_points: Severe asthma signs: accessory muscles, quiet chest, 1-2 word speech, drowsiness, cyanosis.
Inhaler technique with spacer; repeat doses; multiple treatments may be needed.
4x4x4 approach: 4 puffs, 4 breaths each, wait 4 min; no improvement -> evacuate.
Evacuate if not improving or episodes become more frequent/longer.
Distinguish from HAPE (gradual, crackles) and hyperventilation (no wheeze, tingling, spasm).

outcome.summary: Much better at 20 min; camped for observation; symptom-free next morning; trip continued.

must_ask: do you have your inhaler?
can you speak full sentences?
any lips turning blue or drowsiness?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate if not improving with inhaler or worsening; emergency if severe signs.

title: Clumsy, shivering backpacker on a wet 7-12C day in the Smokies

source.title: Case Study: Hypothermia on a Wet Smokies Backpacking Trip

classification.acuity_basis: Improved in 30-45 min with shelter, dry layers, insulation, calories; camped nearby.

presentation.summary: After hours of drizzle and sweaty uphill hiking, a backpacker says he's 'just tired' but is shivering, clumsy with buckles and zippers, quieter than usual and walking slowly and unsteadily.
presentation.last_intake_output: ~1 L water, small lunch, no urination for hours

assessment: possible hypothermia from cold, wet, wind
plan: stop and shelter from wind/rain
dry insulating layers, ground insulation
warm sweet fluids and food if able to swallow
wrapped hot bottles to trunk/armpits
reassess; evacuate if not improving or mental status/coordination worsens
teaching_points: Hypothermia occurs well above freezing with wet, wind, fatigue, and poor intake.
'The umbles': stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles are early signs.
Stop exposure, rewarm, reassess, then change the objective.
Ask whether the group can keep the patient warm while moving.

decision_points.question: Continue to destination?
decision_points.source_decision: No; camp nearby and modify trip

outcome.summary: Shivering and coordination improved over 30-45 min; normal by evening; trip modified.

must_ask: is he shivering?
is he fumbling, stumbling, or slurring?
are his clothes wet?
can you get out of the wind and rain?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate if confusion, shivering stops, or no improvement.

lay_queries: he's shivering and fumbling with zippers in the rain
my friend says he's just tired but he's cold and wet

title: Mountaineering student with wheeze and cough in wildfire haze at 8-11k ft

source.title: Case Study: Asthma During an Introductory Mountaineering Course

classification.acuity_basis: Improved with albuterol; objective abandoned and group descended.

context.weather: early October, clear, dry; wildfire haze day 3

pertinent_history: flew sea level to Reno 4 days earlier

presentation.summary: On an uphill approach in wildfire haze, an experienced hiker develops cough, wheeze, chest tightness and exertional breathlessness she attributed to altitude, so she didn't use her inhaler.
presentation.chief_complaint: cough, wheeze, chest tightness, SOB on exertion

vitals.note: after albuterol; HR decreased, cough/wheeze improved

assessment: possible asthma exacerbation (exercise, smoke, allergen, dry air)
plan: stop ascent, rest
albuterol 2 puffs per prescription
reassess RR and work of breathing
hydrate
antihistamine on request
N95 at rest
evacuate if no improvement, recurrence with minimal exertion, or distress
teaching_points: Improvement after inhaler doesn't equal readiness for strenuous travel.
Capable participants minimize symptoms; watch pace and breathing.
N95s help at rest but are hard to use during exertion.
The easiest exit may be the planned route.

outcome.summary: RR 26 -> 20 with albuterol and rest; group descended.

must_ask: do you have asthma or an inhaler?
wheezing?
is there smoke or a known allergen?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate if not improving or recurrence with minimal exertion.
must_not_recommend: pushing to the summit after one inhaler dose

lay_queries: coughing and wheezing hiking in smoky air

title: Cross-country skier falls on his back with worsening low back pain in single-digit cold

source.title: Case Study: A Hard Fall While Skiing

classification.acuity_basis: Midline lumbar tenderness, transient leg tingling; SAR sled evacuation; spine fractures.

context.weather: clear, no wind, low teens F
context.distance_to_care: 3 mi from trailhead; cell signal on nearby ridge

presentation.summary: Skier falls hard on his back, skis a short way, then collapses gasping. Wind knocked out resolves; he has worsening low back pain and had tingling down both legs for a few minutes.

plan: not a candidate for focused spine assessment (spine pain)
protect spine: packs as head blocks, scarf collar
insulate: layers, boughs, fire, dry socks
send two skiers to ridge to call SAR with GPS location
teaching_points: Spine pain/tenderness rules out field clearance.
Persistently elevated HR may signal shock.
Carry gear for a long wait in winter; plan for worst case.

outcome.summary: SAR arrived by snowmobile ~2 h after fall; sled transport. Several spine fractures without cord injury.
outcome.final_diagnosis: lumbar spine fractures, no cord injury

must_recognize: midline back tenderness + transient neuro symptoms = spine injury
must_ask: does pressing the spine hurt?
any numbness or tingling?
can you insulate him from the snow?
eval.must_escalate: Call SAR; protect spine; prevent hypothermia.
